title: Aerial Lift Safety: Fall Protection, Stability, and Power Lines
summary: Aerial lifts such as scissor lifts, boom lifts, and bucket trucks kill workers every year through falls, tip-overs, and electrocution. This talk covers how to set up, inspect, and work from a lift safely.
talking_points: Inspect the lift before every use: operating and emergency controls, guardrails, fall protection gear, and any leaks of air, hydraulic fluid, or fuel.
Set outriggers, brakes, and wheel chocks every time, even on level ground. Never exceed the manufacturer's slope limit.

On a boom-type lift (articulating or telescoping boom, bucket truck), wear a full-body harness with a lanyard clipped to the manufacturer's anchor point. On a scissor lift, the guardrails are your fall protection: keep them and the gate closed, and wear a harness only if the manufacturer's manual calls for one.
On any lift, stand on the platform floor. Do not climb, sit, or lean over the rails, and never use a ladder or planks to gain height.
Keep the platform gate, chains, or bars closed while working.
Stay clear of overhead power lines and wires. Ask your supervisor to confirm nearby lines are de-energized before you go up.
Do not exceed the rated load. Do not drive with the platform raised unless the lift is built for it.
site_hazards_to_check: Potholes, bumps, soft ground, curbs, or debris in the lift's travel and set-up area
Overhead power lines, energized wires, or other obstructions above the work zone
Missing or damaged guardrails, gates, or platform chains (the fall protection on a scissor lift)
Damaged or missing harness, lanyard, or anchor point on a boom-type lift
Air, hydraulic, or fuel leaks on the machine
discussion_questions: Is today's lift a boom lift or a scissor lift, and what does that mean for the fall protection we use?
What overhead hazards are in our work area, and how far will we stay from them?
What do you do if the lift starts to tip or a control stops responding?

flags: RESOLVED: 29 CFR 1926.451 added. Scissor lifts are regulated by OSHA as mobile scaffolds under 1926.451 (guardrail systems in 1926.451(g)), while 1926.453 (via ANSI A92.2-1969) covers the boom-type lifts and bucket trucks in scope. Both standards are now correctly mapped to the content.

RESOLVED: the blanket harness instruction has been split correctly - boom-type lifts require a full-body harness with lanyard to the manufacturer's anchor point (1926.453(b)(2)(v), as modified by Subpart M), and scissor lifts rely on an intact guardrail system as fall protection with a harness only where the manufacturer's manual requires it. Accurate.

VERIFIED accurate: pre-use inspection of controls, guardrails, fall gear and leaks; set brakes/outriggers/chocks and observe the manufacturer's slope limit (1926.453(b)(2)(vii)); stand on the platform floor, no ladders or planks (1926.453(b)(2)(iv)); keep the gate/chains closed; do not exceed rated load; do not travel elevated unless the lift is designed for it (1926.453(b)(2)(viii)); maintain clearance from overhead lines and confirm de-energized before going up. No numeric tolerances are stated in the talk, so none are in error.
OPTIONAL (non-blocking): consider also citing 29 CFR 1926.452(w) for the mobile-scaffold specifics behind the elevated-travel and caster/brake talking points on scissor lifts.
